questions.question: Consider the infinite-length, discrete-time sequence [latex]x[n] = 0.9^{|n|}[/latex], where [latex]n[/latex] is an integer. The region of convergence of its Z-transform [latex]X(z)[/latex] is given by: (Note: [latex]z[/latex] is a complex variable)
questions.explanation: Split [latex]x[n] = 0.9^{|n|}[/latex] into two parts: Causal part: [latex]0.9^{n}u[n][/latex] ROC: [latex]|z| > 0.9[/latex] Anti-causal part: [latex]0.9^{-n}u[-n-1][/latex] ROC: [latex]|z| < \frac{1}{0.9}[/latex] ROC of bilateral Z-transform = intersection: [latex]0.9 < |z| < \dfrac{1}{0.9}[/latex] Answer: (C)
questions.explanation_html:
Split [latex]x[n] = 0.9^{|n|}[/latex] into two parts:

Causal part: [latex]0.9^{n}u[n][/latex]
ROC: [latex]|z| > 0.9[/latex]
Anti-causal part: [latex]0.9^{-n}u[-n-1][/latex]
ROC: [latex]|z| < \frac{1}{0.9}[/latex]

ROC of bilateral Z-transform = intersection:
[latex]0.9 < |z| < \dfrac{1}{0.9}[/latex]

Answer: (C)

questions.question: Let [latex]x_c(t)[/latex] be any continuous-time periodic signal with period [latex]T[/latex]. It is sampled uniformly with a sampling period [latex]T_s[/latex] where [latex]T_s \neq T[/latex], resulting in the discrete sequence [latex]x[n] = x_c(nT_s)[/latex], where [latex]n[/latex] is an integer. Which one of the following statements is correct about [latex]x[n][/latex]?

options.A: [latex]x[n][/latex] will always be periodic with period [latex]T/T_s[/latex] for all values of [latex]T/T_s[/latex]
options.B: [latex]x[n][/latex] will always be periodic with period [latex]1[/latex] for all values of [latex]T/T_s[/latex]
options.D: [latex]x[n][/latex] will be periodic if and only if [latex]T/T_s[/latex] is a rational number

questions.explanation: For [latex]x[n] = x_c(nT_s)[/latex] to be periodic with integer period [latex]N[/latex]: [latex]x_c(nT_s) = x_c((n+N)T_s)[/latex] This requires [latex]NT_s = kT[/latex] for some integer [latex]k[/latex]. [latex]\Rightarrow \dfrac{T}{T_s} = \dfrac{N}{k} \in \mathbb{Q}[/latex] (rational) [latex]x[n][/latex] is periodic if and only if [latex]T/T_s[/latex] is rational. Answer: (D)
questions.explanation_html:
For [latex]x[n] = x_c(nT_s)[/latex] to be periodic with integer period [latex]N[/latex]:
[latex]x_c(nT_s) = x_c((n+N)T_s)[/latex]

This requires [latex]NT_s = kT[/latex] for some integer [latex]k[/latex].
[latex]\Rightarrow \dfrac{T}{T_s} = \dfrac{N}{k} \in \mathbb{Q}[/latex] (rational)

[latex]x[n][/latex] is periodic if and only if [latex]T/T_s[/latex] is rational.

Answer: (D)

questions.question: Consider a power system with [latex]N[/latex] buses, of which [latex]P[/latex] are generator buses and the remaining [latex]Q[/latex] are load buses (where there is no generation). Assume that there are no reactive power-limit violations at the generator buses. What is the size of the Jacobian matrix in the Newton-Raphson load flow method?
questions.explanation:
Given: A power system has [latex]N[/latex] buses, of which: [latex]P[/latex] are generator buses (including the slack bus) [latex]Q[/latex] are load (PQ) buses Hence,

[latex]
N=P+Q
[/latex] Step 1: Count the unknown voltage angles In the Newton-Raphson load flow method, the voltage angle of the slack bus is known. Therefore, voltage angles of all remaining buses are unknown.

[latex]
\text{Number of angle unknowns}=N-1
[/latex] Step 2: Count the unknown voltage magnitudes Voltage magnitudes are known at generator (PV) buses and at the slack bus. They are unknown only at PQ buses.

Therefore,

[latex]
\text{Number of magnitude unknowns}=Q
[/latex] Step 3: Total number of unknowns [latex]
(N-1)+Q
[/latex] Using [latex]Q=N-P[/latex], [latex]
(N-1)+(N-P)
=
2N-1-P
[/latex] Step 4: Size of the Jacobian matrix The Jacobian matrix is a square matrix whose order equals the total number of unknown variables. Hence,

[latex]
\text{Jacobian Size}
=
(2N-1-P)\times(2N-1-P)
[/latex]
questions.explanation_html:
Given:
A power system has [latex]N[/latex] buses, of which:
[latex]P[/latex] are generator buses (including the slack bus)
[latex]Q[/latex] are load (PQ) buses

Hence, [latex] N=P+Q [/latex]

Step 1: Count the unknown voltage angles
In the Newton-Raphson load flow method, the voltage angle of the slack bus is known.
Therefore, voltage angles of all remaining buses are unknown. [latex] \text{Number of angle unknowns}=N-1 [/latex]

Step 2: Count the unknown voltage magnitudes
Voltage magnitudes are known at generator (PV) buses and at the slack bus.
They are unknown only at PQ buses. Therefore, [latex] \text{Number of magnitude unknowns}=Q [/latex]

Step 3: Total number of unknowns
[latex] (N-1)+Q [/latex]
Using [latex]Q=N-P[/latex],
[latex] (N-1)+(N-P) = 2N-1-P [/latex]

Step 4: Size of the Jacobian matrix
The Jacobian matrix is a square matrix whose order equals the total number of unknown variables.
Hence, [latex] \text{Jacobian Size} = (2N-1-P)\times(2N-1-P) [/latex]

questions.question: The initial three-phase voltage phasors [latex](\bar{V}_A,\ \bar{V}_B,\ \bar{V}_C)[/latex] at a bus of a power network are as shown in Case-1. Due to a disturbance, the bus voltage phasors changed in phase by a small angle [latex]\Delta\theta[/latex], and the magnitudes remained the same as depicted in Case-2. Which one of the following statements is correct about the zero sequence components?

options.A: The zero sequence components in Case-1 and Case-2 have the same phase angle and magnitude
options.B: The magnitude of the zero sequence component in Case-1 is greater than that in Case-2
options.C: The magnitude of the zero sequence component in Case-2 is greater than that in Case-1
options.D: The zero sequence components in Case-1 and Case-2 have the same magnitude but different phase angles

questions.explanation_html:
Concept:
The zero-sequence component of a three-phase set is [latex] V_0=\frac{V_A+V_B+V_C}{3} [/latex]

Case-1:
The phase voltages are [latex] V_A=V_A\angle\theta_A,\qquad V_B=V_B\angle\theta_B,\qquad V_C=V_C\angle\theta_C [/latex]
Therefore,
[latex] V_{0,1} = \frac{V_A\angle\theta_A+V_B\angle\theta_B+V_C\angle\theta_C}{3} [/latex]

Case-2:
Each phasor is rotated by the same angle [latex]\Delta\theta[/latex], while its magnitude remains unchanged.
Hence,
[latex] V_A'=V_A\angle(\theta_A+\Delta\theta) [/latex]
[latex] V_B'=V_B\angle(\theta_B+\Delta\theta) [/latex]
[latex] V_C'=V_C\angle(\theta_C+\Delta\theta) [/latex]
The new zero-sequence component is [latex] V_{0,2} = \frac{V_A'+V_B'+V_C'}{3} [/latex]
Substituting, [latex] V_{0,2} = \frac{ V_A\angle(\theta_A+\Delta\theta) + V_B\angle(\theta_B+\Delta\theta) + V_C\angle(\theta_C+\Delta\theta) }{3} [/latex]
Factoring out [latex]e^{j\Delta\theta}[/latex],
[latex] V_{0,2} = e^{j\Delta\theta} \frac{ V_A\angle\theta_A + V_B\angle\theta_B + V_C\angle\theta_C }{3} [/latex]
[latex] V_{0,2} = e^{j\Delta\theta}V_{0,1} [/latex]

Observation:
Multiplication by [latex]e^{j\Delta\theta}[/latex] rotates a phasor by [latex]\Delta\theta[/latex] but does not change its magnitude.
Therefore,
[latex] |V_{0,2}|=|V_{0,1}| [/latex] and [latex] \angle V_{0,2} = \angle V_{0,1} + \Delta\theta [/latex]

Hence, the zero-sequence components in the two cases have the same magnitude but different phase angles.

questions.question: A certain application requires power at a frequency of 16.67 Hz, while the available grid frequency is 50 Hz. A 3-phase synchronous motor connected to the 50 Hz, 3-phase grid, driving a synchronous generator, is used for this application. Which one of the following combinations is a suitable choice for the number of poles in the motor and generator, respectively?

\dfrac{f_m}{f_g}
=
\dfrac{50}{16.67}
\approx 3
[/latex]

and both machines run at the same speed,

[latex]
\dfrac{P_m}{P_g}=3
[/latex] So simply choose the option where the motor poles : generator poles = 3 : 1.
questions.explanation_html:
Synchronous speed formula: [latex]N_s = \dfrac{120f}{P}[/latex]

Motor on 50 Hz grid with [latex]P_m = 6[/latex] poles:
[latex]N_s = \dfrac{120 \times 50}{6} = 1000[/latex] rpm

Generator must produce 16.67 Hz at 1000 rpm:
[latex]f_g = \dfrac{P_g \times N_s}{120} = 16.67[/latex]

[latex] \dfrac{f_m}{f_g} = \dfrac{50}{16.67} \approx 3 [/latex] and both machines run at the same speed, [latex] \dfrac{P_m}{P_g}=3 [/latex]
So simply choose the option where the motor poles : generator poles = 3 : 1.

questions.question: Which one of the following options is correct regarding the typical double-squirrel-cage structure used in induction motors?

options.A: At starting, a larger portion of the rotor current flows in the outer cage
options.B: At starting, a larger portion of the rotor current flows in the inner cage
options.C: At rated speed, most of the rotor current flows in the outer cage
options.D: The purpose of the double-squirrel-cage structure is to lower the effective rotor resistance at starting

questions.explanation:
Concept of Double-Squirrel-Cage Induction Motor A double-squirrel-cage rotor consists of two cages: 1. Outer cage - High resistance - Low reactance 2. Inner cage - Low resistance - High reactance At starting: The slip is

[latex]
s=1
[/latex]. 

Therefore, rotor frequency is maximum, and rotor reactance becomes significant.

Since the inner cage has high reactance, its impedance is large: [latex]
Z_{\text{inner}}
=
R_{\text{inner}}
+
jX_{\text{inner}}
[/latex]

with

[latex]
X_{\text{inner}} \gg X_{\text{outer}}
[/latex] Hence, most of the rotor current flows through the outer cage, which has lower impedance.

The high resistance of the outer cage provides a high starting torque. At rated speed: The slip is very small.

Hence rotor frequency is low and rotor reactance becomes negligible.

Current distribution is then determined mainly by resistance.

Since

[latex]
R_{\text{inner}} < R_{\text{outer}}
[/latex]

most of the rotor current flows through the inner cage.

Thus the motor behaves like a low-resistance rotor during normal operation, giving good efficiency. The purpose is actually to obtain high effective rotor resistance at starting and low effective rotor resistance during normal running .
questions.explanation_html:
Concept of Double-Squirrel-Cage Induction Motor

A double-squirrel-cage rotor consists of two cages:
1. Outer cage
- High resistance
- Low reactance

2. Inner cage
- Low resistance
- High reactance

At starting:
The slip is [latex] s=1 [/latex]. Therefore, rotor frequency is maximum, and rotor reactance becomes significant. Since the inner cage has high reactance, its impedance is large:
[latex] Z_{\text{inner}} = R_{\text{inner}} + jX_{\text{inner}} [/latex] with [latex] X_{\text{inner}} \gg X_{\text{outer}} [/latex]
Hence, most of the rotor current flows through the outer cage, which has lower impedance. The high resistance of the outer cage provides a high starting torque.

At rated speed:
The slip is very small. Hence rotor frequency is low and rotor reactance becomes negligible. Current distribution is then determined mainly by resistance. Since [latex] R_{\text{inner}} < R_{\text{outer}} [/latex] most of the rotor current flows through the inner cage. Thus the motor behaves like a low-resistance rotor during normal operation, giving good efficiency.

The purpose is actually to obtain high effective rotor resistance at starting and low effective rotor resistance during normal running.

A synchronous generator connected to an infinite bus operates with: [latex] P=\frac{EV}{X_s}\sin\delta [/latex] where [latex] E [/latex] = internal generated emf, [latex] V [/latex] = infinite-bus voltage, [latex] X_s [/latex] = synchronous reactance, [latex] \delta [/latex] = load angle.

questions.question: A time-limited waveform [latex]g(x)[/latex] is specified as follows: [latex]g(x) = \begin{cases} -k, & -\pi < x \leq 0 \\ +k, & 0 < x \leq \pi \\ 0, & \text{otherwise} \end{cases}[/latex] A new waveform [latex]f(x)[/latex] is constructed from [latex]g(x)[/latex] as follows: [latex]f(x) = \displaystyle\sum_{m=-\infty}^{\infty} g(x + 2\pi m)[/latex], for all [latex]x \in \mathbb{R}[/latex] The sum of the coefficients of the third harmonics of the sine and cosine terms in the trigonometric Fourier series expansion of [latex]f(x)[/latex] is [latex]\dfrac{2}{3\pi}[/latex]. What is the value of [latex]k[/latex]?
questions.explanation:
A periodic function is formed as

[latex]
f(x)=\sum_{m=-\infty}^{\infty}g(x+2\pi m),
[/latex]

which is a periodic function with period

[latex]
2\pi.
[/latex] Step 1: Identify the symmetry Since

[latex]
f(-x)=-f(x),
[/latex]

the function is odd .

Hence, All cosine coefficients are zero. Only sine coefficients are present. Therefore,

[latex]
a_n=0.
[/latex] Step 2: Calculate the sine coefficients The sine coefficient is

[latex]
b_n=\dfrac{1}{\pi}\int_{-\pi}^{\pi}f(x)\sin(nx)\,dx.
[/latex] Substituting the given waveform, [latex]
b_n
=
\dfrac{1}{\pi}
\left[
\int_{-\pi}^{0}(-k)\sin(nx)\,dx
+
\int_{0}^{\pi}k\sin(nx)\,dx
\right].
[/latex] Since the two integrals are equal, [latex]
b_n
=
\dfrac{2k}{\pi}
\int_{0}^{\pi}\sin(nx)\,dx.
[/latex] Now,

[latex]
\int_{0}^{\pi}\sin(nx)\,dx
=
\dfrac{1-(-1)^n}{n}.
[/latex] Hence,

[latex]
b_n
=
\dfrac{2k}{n\pi}
\left(1-(-1)^n\right).
[/latex] For odd harmonics,

[latex]
(-1)^n=-1,
[/latex] therefore,

[latex]
b_n=\dfrac{4k}{n\pi}.
[/latex] Step 3: Third harmonic For

[latex]
n=3,
[/latex] [latex]
a_3=0,
[/latex]

and

[latex]
b_3=\dfrac{4k}{3\pi}.
[/latex] The question states that the sum of the third-harmonic cosine and sine coefficients is [latex]
a_3+b_3=\dfrac{2}{3\pi}.
[/latex] Since

[latex]
a_3=0,
[/latex] [latex]
\dfrac{4k}{3\pi}
=
\dfrac{2}{3\pi}.
[/latex] Therefore,

[latex]
4k=2
[/latex] [latex]
k=\dfrac{1}{2}.

questions.explanation_html:
A periodic function is formed as [latex] f(x)=\sum_{m=-\infty}^{\infty}g(x+2\pi m), [/latex] which is a periodic function with period [latex] 2\pi. [/latex]

Step 1: Identify the symmetry
Since [latex] f(-x)=-f(x), [/latex] the function is odd. Hence,
  • All cosine coefficients are zero.
  • Only sine coefficients are present.
Therefore, [latex] a_n=0. [/latex]

Step 2: Calculate the sine coefficients
The sine coefficient is [latex] b_n=\dfrac{1}{\pi}\int_{-\pi}^{\pi}f(x)\sin(nx)\,dx. [/latex]
Substituting the given waveform,
[latex] b_n = \dfrac{1}{\pi} \left[ \int_{-\pi}^{0}(-k)\sin(nx)\,dx + \int_{0}^{\pi}k\sin(nx)\,dx \right]. [/latex]
Since the two integrals are equal,
[latex] b_n = \dfrac{2k}{\pi} \int_{0}^{\pi}\sin(nx)\,dx. [/latex]
Now, [latex] \int_{0}^{\pi}\sin(nx)\,dx = \dfrac{1-(-1)^n}{n}. [/latex]
Hence, [latex] b_n = \dfrac{2k}{n\pi} \left(1-(-1)^n\right). [/latex]
For odd harmonics, [latex] (-1)^n=-1, [/latex]
therefore, [latex] b_n=\dfrac{4k}{n\pi}. [/latex]

Step 3: Third harmonic
For [latex] n=3, [/latex]
[latex] a_3=0, [/latex] and [latex] b_3=\dfrac{4k}{3\pi}. [/latex]
The question states that the sum of the third-harmonic cosine and sine coefficients is
[latex] a_3+b_3=\dfrac{2}{3\pi}. [/latex]
Since [latex] a_3=0, [/latex]
[latex] \dfrac{4k}{3\pi} = \dfrac{2}{3\pi}. [/latex]
Therefore, [latex] 4k=2 [/latex]
[latex] k=\dfrac{1}{2}. [/latex]

questions.question: The operating characteristic of a reactance relay is given by [latex]X \leq 1\ \Omega[/latex], where [latex]X[/latex] is the reactance calculated by the relay. Its operating characteristic in the admittance plane ([latex]G[/latex]-[latex]B[/latex] plane, where [latex]G[/latex] and [latex]B[/latex] denote conductance and susceptance, respectively, expressed in [latex]\mho[/latex]) is given by:
questions.explanation:
The operating characteristic of the reactance relay is

[latex]
X \leq 1~\Omega
[/latex]

where [latex]X[/latex] is the reactance seen by the relay. The impedance seen by the relay is

[latex]
Z=R+jX
[/latex] The corresponding admittance is

[latex]
Y=\dfrac{1}{Z}=G+jB
[/latex]

where [latex]
G=\dfrac{R}{R^2+X^2},
\qquad
B=-\dfrac{X}{R^2+X^2}
[/latex] Since

[latex]
R=\dfrac{G}{G^2+B^2},
\qquad
X=-\dfrac{B}{G^2+B^2}
[/latex]

substitute into the relay characteristic

[latex]
X\le 1
[/latex]

to obtain

[latex]
-\dfrac{B}{G^2+B^2}\le 1
[/latex] Rearranging,

[latex]
G^2+B^2+B\ge 0
[/latex] Completing the square, [latex]
G^2+\left(B+\dfrac{1}{2}\right)^2\ge\dfrac14
[/latex] Multiplying both sides by 4, [latex]
4G^2+4\left(B+\dfrac{1}{2}\right)^2\ge 1
[/latex] or [latex]
4G^2+(2B+1)^2\ge 1
[/latex] Hence,

[latex]
G^2+\left(B+\dfrac{1}{2}\right)^2\ge\dfrac{1}{4}
[/latex]
questions.explanation_html:
The operating characteristic of the reactance relay is [latex] X \leq 1~\Omega [/latex] where [latex]X[/latex] is the reactance seen by the relay.

The impedance seen by the relay is [latex] Z=R+jX [/latex]
The corresponding admittance is [latex] Y=\dfrac{1}{Z}=G+jB [/latex] where
[latex] G=\dfrac{R}{R^2+X^2}, \qquad B=-\dfrac{X}{R^2+X^2} [/latex]

Since [latex] R=\dfrac{G}{G^2+B^2}, \qquad X=-\dfrac{B}{G^2+B^2} [/latex] substitute into the relay characteristic [latex] X\le 1 [/latex] to obtain [latex] -\dfrac{B}{G^2+B^2}\le 1 [/latex]
Rearranging, [latex] G^2+B^2+B\ge 0 [/latex]
Completing the square,
[latex] G^2+\left(B+\dfrac{1}{2}\right)^2\ge\dfrac14 [/latex]
Multiplying both sides by 4,
[latex] 4G^2+4\left(B+\dfrac{1}{2}\right)^2\ge 1 [/latex]
or
[latex] 4G^2+(2B+1)^2\ge 1 [/latex]
Hence, [latex] G^2+\left(B+\dfrac{1}{2}\right)^2\ge\dfrac{1}{4} [/latex]

questions.question: A three-phase two-winding transformer has a voltage transformation ratio [latex]\dfrac{V_P}{V_S} = 0.866 + j0.5[/latex], where [latex]V_P[/latex] is the primary side voltage in p.u., and [latex]V_S[/latex] is the secondary side voltage in p.u. [latex]I_P[/latex] and [latex]I_S[/latex] represent the currents injected into the primary and secondary sides of the transformer, respectively. The admittance corresponding to the leakage impedance of the transformer referred to the secondary is [latex]y_t[/latex] p.u. Neglect the magnetizing branch. The Y bus representation of this transformer is:
questions.explanation:
The transformer has a voltage transformation ratio

[latex]
\dfrac{V_P}{V_S}=0.866+j0.5
[/latex] Let

[latex]
a=0.866+j0.5
[/latex] The leakage impedance referred to the secondary side is

[latex]
y \text{ p.u.}
[/latex]

,where [latex]y[/latex] is the series admittance. For a transformer having an off-nominal complex tap ratio [latex]a[/latex], the branch equations are [latex]
I_P=\dfrac{y}{|a|^2}V_P-\dfrac{y}{a^*}V_S
[/latex] [latex]
I_S=-\dfrac{y}{a}V_P+yV_S
[/latex] where [latex]a^*[/latex] is the complex conjugate of [latex]a[/latex]. Since

[latex]
a=0.866+j0.5,
\qquad
|a|=\sqrt{0.866^2+0.5^2}=1
[/latex] therefore,

[latex]
|a|^2=1
[/latex] Also,

[latex]
a^*=0.866-j0.5
[/latex] Since [latex]|a|=1[/latex],

[latex]
\dfrac{1}{a}=a^*=0.866-j0.5
[/latex]

and

[latex]
\dfrac{1}{a^*}=a=0.866+j0.5
[/latex] Substituting these values,

[latex]
I_P
=
yV_P
-
\dfrac{y}{0.866-j0.5}V_S
[/latex]

and

[latex]
I_S
=
-\dfrac{y}{0.866+j0.5}V_P
+yV_S
[/latex] Hence, the Y-bus representation is

[latex]
\begin{bmatrix}
I_P\\
I_S
\end{bmatrix}
=
\begin{bmatrix}
y & -\dfrac{y}{0.866-j0.5}\\[8pt]
-\dfrac{y}{0.866+j0.5} & y
\end{bmatrix}
\begin{bmatrix}
V_P\\
V_S
\end{bmatrix}
[/latex]
questions.explanation_html:
The transformer has a voltage transformation ratio [latex] \dfrac{V_P}{V_S}=0.866+j0.5 [/latex]
Let [latex] a=0.866+j0.5 [/latex]
The leakage impedance referred to the secondary side is [latex] y \text{ p.u.} [/latex] ,where [latex]y[/latex] is the series admittance.

For a transformer having an off-nominal complex tap ratio [latex]a[/latex], the branch equations are
[latex] I_P=\dfrac{y}{|a|^2}V_P-\dfrac{y}{a^*}V_S [/latex]
[latex] I_S=-\dfrac{y}{a}V_P+yV_S [/latex]
where [latex]a^*[/latex] is the complex conjugate of [latex]a[/latex].

Since [latex] a=0.866+j0.5, \qquad |a|=\sqrt{0.866^2+0.5^2}=1 [/latex]
therefore, [latex] |a|^2=1 [/latex]
Also, [latex] a^*=0.866-j0.5 [/latex]
Since [latex]|a|=1[/latex], [latex] \dfrac{1}{a}=a^*=0.866-j0.5 [/latex] and [latex] \dfrac{1}{a^*}=a=0.866+j0.5 [/latex]

Substituting these values, [latex] I_P = yV_P - \dfrac{y}{0.866-j0.5}V_S [/latex] and [latex] I_S = -\dfrac{y}{0.866+j0.5}V_P +yV_S [/latex]
Hence, the Y-bus representation is [latex] \begin{bmatrix} I_P\\ I_S \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} y & -\dfrac{y}{0.866-j0.5}\\[8pt] -\dfrac{y}{0.866+j0.5} & y \end{bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix} V_P\\ V_S \end{bmatrix} [/latex]

questions.question: An electrical component has voltage drop [latex]v = V_m\sin(\omega t)[/latex], when the current through it is [latex]i = I_m\sin(\omega t - \theta)[/latex]. What is the average power dissipated over a half cycle corresponding to [latex]\omega[/latex]?
questions.explanation:
The instantaneous power is

[latex]
p=vi
\;=\;
V_mI_m\sin(\omega t)\sin(\omega t-\theta)
[/latex] Using the trigonometric identity

[latex]
\sin A\sin B=\dfrac{1}{2}\left[\cos(A-B)-\cos(A+B)\right],
[/latex]

we get

[latex]
p
=
\dfrac{V_mI_m}{2}
\left[
\cos\theta
-
\cos(2\omega t-\theta)
\right]
[/latex] The average power over one half-cycle is

[latex]
P_{\text{avg}}
=
\dfrac{1}{T/2}
\int_{0}^{T/2}
p\,dt
[/latex] Substituting the expression for [latex]p[/latex], [latex]
P_{\text{avg}}
=
\dfrac{1}{T/2}
\int_{0}^{T/2}
\dfrac{V_mI_m}{2}
\left[
\cos\theta
-
\cos(2\omega t-\theta)
\right]dt
[/latex] Separating the two terms,

[latex]
P_{\text{avg}}
=
\dfrac{V_mI_m}{T}
\left[
\cos\theta
\int_{0}^{T/2}dt
-
\int_{0}^{T/2}\cos(2\omega t-\theta)\,dt
\right]
[/latex] The first integral is

[latex]
\int_{0}^{T/2}dt=\dfrac{T}{2}
[/latex] For the second integral,

[latex]
\int_{0}^{T/2}\cos(2\omega t-\theta)\,dt
=
\dfrac{1}{2\omega}
\left[
\sin(2\omega t-\theta)
\right]_{0}^{T/2}
[/latex] Since

[latex]
\omega T=2\pi,
[/latex]

we have

[latex]
2\omega\left(\dfrac{T}{2}\right)=2\pi
[/latex] Therefore,

[latex]
\sin(2\pi-\theta)=\sin(-\theta),
[/latex]

and hence

[latex]
\left[
\sin(2\omega t-\theta)
\right]_{0}^{T/2}
=
\sin(-\theta)-\sin(-\theta)=0
[/latex] Thus, the second integral is zero. Hence, [latex]
P_{\text{avg}}
=
\dfrac{V_mI_m}{T}
\left(
\cos\theta\cdot\dfrac{T}{2}
\right)
[/latex] [latex]
P_{\text{avg}}
=
\dfrac{V_mI_m}{2}\cos\theta
[/latex]
questions.explanation_html:
The instantaneous power is [latex] p=vi \;=\; V_mI_m\sin(\omega t)\sin(\omega t-\theta) [/latex]
Using the trigonometric identity [latex] \sin A\sin B=\dfrac{1}{2}\left[\cos(A-B)-\cos(A+B)\right], [/latex] we get [latex] p = \dfrac{V_mI_m}{2} \left[ \cos\theta - \cos(2\omega t-\theta) \right] [/latex]

The average power over one half-cycle is [latex] P_{\text{avg}} = \dfrac{1}{T/2} \int_{0}^{T/2} p\,dt [/latex]
Substituting the expression for [latex]p[/latex],
[latex] P_{\text{avg}} = \dfrac{1}{T/2} \int_{0}^{T/2} \dfrac{V_mI_m}{2} \left[ \cos\theta - \cos(2\omega t-\theta) \right]dt [/latex]

Separating the two terms, [latex] P_{\text{avg}} = \dfrac{V_mI_m}{T} \left[ \cos\theta \int_{0}^{T/2}dt - \int_{0}^{T/2}\cos(2\omega t-\theta)\,dt \right] [/latex]
The first integral is [latex] \int_{0}^{T/2}dt=\dfrac{T}{2} [/latex]
For the second integral, [latex] \int_{0}^{T/2}\cos(2\omega t-\theta)\,dt = \dfrac{1}{2\omega} \left[ \sin(2\omega t-\theta) \right]_{0}^{T/2} [/latex]
Since [latex] \omega T=2\pi, [/latex] we have [latex] 2\omega\left(\dfrac{T}{2}\right)=2\pi [/latex]
Therefore, [latex] \sin(2\pi-\theta)=\sin(-\theta), [/latex] and hence [latex] \left[ \sin(2\omega t-\theta) \right]_{0}^{T/2} = \sin(-\theta)-\sin(-\theta)=0 [/latex]
Thus, the second integral is zero.

Hence,
[latex] P_{\text{avg}} = \dfrac{V_mI_m}{T} \left( \cos\theta\cdot\dfrac{T}{2} \right) [/latex]
[latex] P_{\text{avg}} = \dfrac{V_mI_m}{2}\cos\theta [/latex]

questions.question: Consider the second-order differential equation [latex]\dfrac{d^{2}y}{dx^{2}} + \dfrac{dy}{dx} + y = 0[/latex] with initial conditions [latex]y(0)=1[/latex], [latex]\dfrac{dy}{dx}\Big|_{x=0}=1[/latex] The solution is given by

questions.explanation_html:
Characteristic equation: [latex]r^2 + r + 1 = 0[/latex]
[latex]r = \dfrac{-1 \pm \sqrt{1-4}}{2} = -\dfrac{1}{2} \pm j\dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2}[/latex]

General solution: [latex]y = e^{-x/2}\!\left(C_1\cos\dfrac{\sqrt{3}x}{2} + C_2\sin\dfrac{\sqrt{3}x}{2}\right)[/latex]

Apply [latex]y(0) = 1[/latex]: [latex]C_1 = 1[/latex]

[latex]\Rightarrow -\dfrac{1}{2} + C_2\dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2} = 1 \Rightarrow C_2 = \dfrac{3}{\sqrt{3}} = \sqrt{3}[/latex]

questions.question: The figure shows an arbitrarily shaped planar conducting loop A in the XY plane. Two nonintersecting regions with areas [latex]a_1[/latex] and [latex]a_2[/latex] within the loop are subjected to magnetic fields [latex]\vec{B}_1 = \dfrac{m}{\sqrt{2}}\sin(\omega t)(1\hat{x} + 0\hat{y} +1\hat{z})[/latex] [latex]\vec{B}_2 = -\dfrac{n}{\sqrt{2}}\cos(2\omega t + \pi/4)(0\hat{x} + 1\hat{y} + 1\hat{z})[/latex] What is the expression for the induced rms voltage in loop A?

Flux through [latex]a_1[/latex]: [latex]\Phi_1 = \vec{B}_1 \cdot \hat{z} \cdot a_1 = \dfrac{m}{\sqrt{2}}\sin(\omega t) \cdot a_1[/latex] EMF[latex]_1 = -\dfrac{d\Phi_1}{dt} = -\dfrac{ma_1\omega}{\sqrt{2}}\cos(\omega t)[/latex] RMS[latex]_1 = \dfrac{ma_1\omega}{\sqrt{2}\cdot\sqrt{2}} = \dfrac{ma_1\omega}{2}[/latex] Flux through [latex]a_2[/latex]: [latex]\Phi_2 = -\dfrac{n}{\sqrt{2}}\cos(2\omega t + \pi/4) \cdot a_2[/latex] EMF[latex]_2 = -\dfrac{d\Phi_2}{dt} = -\dfrac{2na_2\omega}{\sqrt{2}}\sin(2\omega t + \pi/4)[/latex] RMS[latex]_2 = \dfrac{2na_2\omega}{\sqrt{2}\cdot\sqrt{2}} = na_2\omega[/latex] Different frequencies -> total RMS by Parseval: [latex]V_{rms} = \sqrt{\text{RMS}_1^2 + \text{RMS}_2^2} = \sqrt{\dfrac{m^2a_1^2\omega^2}{4} + n^2a_2^2\omega^2} = \sqrt{\dfrac{m^2a_1^2\omega^2 + 4n^2a_2^2\omega^2}{4}}[/latex]

Loop is in XY plane -> normal is [latex]\hat{z}[/latex].

[latex]\Phi_1 = \vec{B}_1 \cdot \hat{z} \cdot a_1 = \dfrac{m}{\sqrt{2}}\sin(\omega t) \cdot a_1[/latex]
EMF[latex]_1 = -\dfrac{d\Phi_1}{dt} = -\dfrac{ma_1\omega}{\sqrt{2}}\cos(\omega t)[/latex]
RMS[latex]_1 = \dfrac{ma_1\omega}{\sqrt{2}\cdot\sqrt{2}} = \dfrac{ma_1\omega}{2}[/latex]

[latex]\det(\lambda I - A) = \lambda(\lambda - a) + ab = \lambda^2 - a\lambda + ab[/latex]

Desired poles at [latex]-2 \pm j3[/latex] -> desired characteristic polynomial:
[latex](\lambda+2-j3)(\lambda+2+j3) = \lambda^2 + 4\lambda + 13[/latex]

Matching coefficients:
[latex]-a = 4 \Rightarrow a = -4[/latex]
[latex]ab = 13 \Rightarrow b = \dfrac{13}{-4} = -3.25[/latex]

questions.question: A system is represented in state-space form ([latex]u[/latex]: input, [latex]\mathbf{x}[/latex]: state vector, [latex]y[/latex]: output): [latex]\dot{\mathbf{x}} = \begin{bmatrix}1&2\\-3&0\end{bmatrix}\mathbf{x} + \begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 2\end{bmatrix}u[/latex], [latex]\ y = [1\ \ 2]\,\mathbf{x}[/latex] Consider the new state vector [latex]\mathbf{z} = \begin{bmatrix}2&1\\-1&0\end{bmatrix}\mathbf{x}[/latex] What is the state-space representation of the system in terms of the new state vector [latex]\mathbf{z}[/latex]?
questions.explanation: Let [latex]T = \begin{bmatrix}2&1\\-1&0\end{bmatrix}[/latex], so [latex]\mathbf{z} = T\mathbf{x}[/latex]. [latex]T^{-1} = \dfrac{1}{\det T}\begin{bmatrix}0&-1\\1&2\end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix}0&-1\\1&2\end{bmatrix}[/latex] (since [latex]\det T = 0-(-1)=1[/latex]) New system matrix: [latex]A_z = T A T^{-1}[/latex] [latex]AT^{-1} = \begin{bmatrix}1&2\\-3&0\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}0&-1\\1&2\end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix}2&3\\0&3\end{bmatrix}[/latex] [latex]A_z = \begin{bmatrix}2&1\\-1&0\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}2&3\\0&3\end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix}4&9\\-2&-3\end{bmatrix}[/latex] New input matrix: [latex]B_z = TB = \begin{bmatrix}2&1\\-1&0\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}1\\2\end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix}4\\-1\end{bmatrix}[/latex] New output matrix: [latex]C_z = CT^{-1} = [1\ \ 2]\begin{bmatrix}0&-1\\1&2\end{bmatrix} = [2\ \ 3][/latex] Answer: (C)
questions.explanation_html:
Let [latex]T = \begin{bmatrix}2&1\\-1&0\end{bmatrix}[/latex], so [latex]\mathbf{z} = T\mathbf{x}[/latex].

[latex]T^{-1} = \dfrac{1}{\det T}\begin{bmatrix}0&-1\\1&2\end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix}0&-1\\1&2\end{bmatrix}[/latex] (since [latex]\det T = 0-(-1)=1[/latex])

New system matrix:
[latex]A_z = T A T^{-1}[/latex]
[latex]AT^{-1} = \begin{bmatrix}1&2\\-3&0\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}0&-1\\1&2\end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix}2&3\\0&3\end{bmatrix}[/latex]
[latex]A_z = \begin{bmatrix}2&1\\-1&0\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}2&3\\0&3\end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix}4&9\\-2&-3\end{bmatrix}[/latex]

New input matrix:
[latex]B_z = TB = \begin{bmatrix}2&1\\-1&0\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}1\\2\end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix}4\\-1\end{bmatrix}[/latex]

New output matrix:
[latex]C_z = CT^{-1} = [1\ \ 2]\begin{bmatrix}0&-1\\1&2\end{bmatrix} = [2\ \ 3][/latex]

Answer: (C)

questions.question: Consider an [latex]n \times n[/latex] orthogonal matrix [latex]A[/latex] with real entries and each column having unit Euclidean norm. Which of the following statements is/are correct?

options.A: The value of the determinant of [latex]A[/latex] is either [latex]+1[/latex] or [latex]-1[/latex]
options.C: [latex]\|A\mathbf{x}\| = \|\mathbf{x}\|[/latex] for all [latex]\mathbf{x}\in\mathbb{R}^n[/latex], where [latex]\|\mathbf{x}\|[/latex]  denotes the Euclidean norm of [latex]x[/latex], and [latex](A\mathbf{x})^T(A\mathbf{y}) \neq \mathbf{x}^T\mathbf{y}[/latex], for all distinct [latex]\mathbf{x},\mathbf{y}\in\mathbb{R}^n[/latex]
options.D: [latex]\|A\mathbf{x}\| = \|\mathbf{x}\|[/latex] for all [latex]\mathbf{x}\in\mathbb{R}^n[/latex], where [latex]\|\mathbf{x}\|[/latex]  denotes the Euclidean norm of [latex]x[/latex], and [latex](A\mathbf{x})^T(A\mathbf{y}) = \mathbf{x}^T\mathbf{y}[/latex], for all  [latex]\mathbf{x},\mathbf{y}\in\mathbb{R}^n[/latex]

questions.explanation: For real orthogonal matrix [latex]A[/latex]: [latex]A^T A = I[/latex] (A) [latex](\det A)^2 = \det(A^T A) = \det I = 1 \Rightarrow \det A = \pm 1[/latex] (B) If [latex]A\mathbf{v} = \lambda\mathbf{v}[/latex], then [latex]|\lambda|^2\|\mathbf{v}\|^2 = \|A\mathbf{v}\|^2 = \|\mathbf{v}\|^2 \Rightarrow |\lambda| = 1[/latex] (C) [latex]\|A\mathbf{x}\| = \|\mathbf{x}\|[/latex] is TRUE, but [latex](A\mathbf{x})^T(A\mathbf{y}) = \mathbf{x}^T A^T A\mathbf{y} = \mathbf{x}^T\mathbf{y}\rightarrow [/latex]  the inequality part is FALSE (D) Both [latex]\|A\mathbf{x}\| = \|\mathbf{x}\|[/latex] and [latex](A\mathbf{x})^T(A\mathbf{y}) = \mathbf{x}^T\mathbf{y}[/latex] are TRUE Answer: (A), (B), (D)
questions.explanation_html:
For real orthogonal matrix [latex]A[/latex]: [latex]A^T A = I[/latex]

(A) [latex](\det A)^2 = \det(A^T A) = \det I = 1 \Rightarrow \det A = \pm 1[/latex]

(B) If [latex]A\mathbf{v} = \lambda\mathbf{v}[/latex], then [latex]|\lambda|^2\|\mathbf{v}\|^2 = \|A\mathbf{v}\|^2 = \|\mathbf{v}\|^2 \Rightarrow |\lambda| = 1[/latex]

(C) [latex]\|A\mathbf{x}\| = \|\mathbf{x}\|[/latex] is TRUE, but [latex](A\mathbf{x})^T(A\mathbf{y}) = \mathbf{x}^T A^T A\mathbf{y} = \mathbf{x}^T\mathbf{y}\rightarrow [/latex] the inequality part is FALSE

(D) Both [latex]\|A\mathbf{x}\| = \|\mathbf{x}\|[/latex] and [latex](A\mathbf{x})^T(A\mathbf{y}) = \mathbf{x}^T\mathbf{y}[/latex] are TRUE

Answer: (A), (B), (D)

questions.question: Consider the system of linear equations: [latex]A\mathbf{x} = \mathbf{b}[/latex], where [latex]A[/latex] is an [latex]n \times n[/latex] matrix, and [latex]\mathbf{x}[/latex] and [latex]\mathbf{b}[/latex] are [latex]n[/latex]-dimensional column vectors. Suppose this system of equations has a unique solution. Which of the following statements is/are correct?

options.B: The system of equations [latex]A^m\mathbf{x} = \mathbf{b}[/latex] also has a unique solution for [latex]m = 1, 2, 3, \ldots[/latex]

questions.explanation: Unique solution [latex]\Rightarrow A[/latex] is invertible ([latex]\det A \neq 0[/latex]). (A) Invertible [latex]\Rightarrow A^{-1}[/latex] exists - True (B) [latex]A[/latex] invertible [latex]\Rightarrow A^m[/latex] invertible for all [latex]m \geq 1[/latex] [latex]\Rightarrow A^m\mathbf{x} = \mathbf{b}[/latex] has unique solution [latex]\mathbf{x} = (A^m)^{-1}\mathbf{b}[/latex] - True (C) [latex]A[/latex] invertible [latex]\Rightarrow \text{rank}(A) = n[/latex]; [latex]A^m[/latex] invertible [latex]\Rightarrow \text{rank}(A^m) = n[/latex] - True (D) Unique solution requires [latex]\text{rank}(A) = \text{rank}([A|\mathbf{b}]) = n[/latex], NOT [latex]<[/latex]. (D) contradicts unique solution - False Answer: (A), (B), (C)
questions.explanation_html:
Unique solution [latex]\Rightarrow A[/latex] is invertible ([latex]\det A \neq 0[/latex]).

(A) Invertible [latex]\Rightarrow A^{-1}[/latex] exists - True

(B) [latex]A[/latex] invertible [latex]\Rightarrow A^m[/latex] invertible for all [latex]m \geq 1[/latex] [latex]\Rightarrow A^m\mathbf{x} = \mathbf{b}[/latex] has unique solution [latex]\mathbf{x} = (A^m)^{-1}\mathbf{b}[/latex] - True

(C) [latex]A[/latex] invertible [latex]\Rightarrow \text{rank}(A) = n[/latex]; [latex]A^m[/latex] invertible [latex]\Rightarrow \text{rank}(A^m) = n[/latex] - True

(D) Unique solution requires [latex]\text{rank}(A) = \text{rank}([A|\mathbf{b}]) = n[/latex], NOT [latex]<[/latex]. (D) contradicts unique solution - False

questions.question: The resistance values of the Wheatstone bridge shown are: [latex]P = 2000\ \Omega[/latex], [latex]Q = 500\ \Omega[/latex], [latex]R = 3000\ \Omega[/latex] The battery voltage [latex]E = 50[/latex] V. The battery has an internal resistance of 1 [latex]\Omega[/latex] and the Galvanometer (G) has a resistance of 50 [latex]\Omega[/latex]. The value of the resistance [latex]S[/latex] for balanced condition is _____________ [latex]\Omega[/latex] (Answer in integer)
questions.explanation: At balance, galvanometer current = 0 (no current through G). Wheatstone bridge balance condition: [latex]\dfrac{P}{Q} = \dfrac{R}{S}[/latex] [latex]S = \dfrac{R \times Q}{P} = \dfrac{3000 \times 500}{2000} = \dfrac{1500000}{2000} = 750\ \Omega[/latex] Note: Internal resistance and galvanometer resistance do not affect the balance condition.
questions.explanation_html:
At balance, galvanometer current = 0 (no current through G).

Wheatstone bridge balance condition:
[latex]\dfrac{P}{Q} = \dfrac{R}{S}[/latex]

[latex]S = \dfrac{R \times Q}{P} = \dfrac{3000 \times 500}{2000} = \dfrac{1500000}{2000} = 750\ \Omega[/latex]

Note: Internal resistance and galvanometer resistance do not affect the balance condition.

questions.question: A system with two generators G1 and G2 (without generator limits) is shown. The total load on the system is 1184 MW.  The expressions for the cost of generation ([latex]C_1[/latex] and [latex]C_2[/latex]) and real power loss ([latex]P_{Loss}[/latex]) are as follows: [latex]C_1(P_{G1}) = 1000 + 50P_{G1} + 0.01(P_{G1})^2 Rs/MWh[/latex] [latex]C_2(P_{G2}) = 2000 + 50P_{G2} + 0.001(P_{G2})^2 Rs/MWh[/latex] [latex]P_{Loss} = 0.001(P_{G2} - 50)^2  MW[/latex] When the generators are operating at their optimal generation, meeting the total load requirement, the real power loss in the system is ________ MW (Round off to one decimal place) Consider the Lagrange multiplier [latex]\lambda = 70.25[/latex] for optimal generation.
questions.explanation: Optimal dispatch conditions: For G1 (no transmission loss from G1): [latex]\lambda = \dfrac{\partial C_1}{\partial P_{G1}} = 50 + 0.02P_{G1}[/latex] [latex]70.25 = 50 + 0.02P_{G1} \Rightarrow P_{G1} = 1012.5[/latex] MW For G2 (with loss): [latex]\dfrac{\partial P_L}{\partial P_{G2}} = 0.002(P_{G2}-50)[/latex] Penalty factor condition: [latex]70.25(1 - 0.002(P_{G2}-50)) = 50 + 0.002P_{G2}[/latex] [latex]70.25 - 0.1405P_{G2} + 7.025 = 50 + 0.002P_{G2}[/latex] [latex]P_{G2}(0.1405 + 0.002) = 27.275 \Rightarrow P_{G2} \approx 191.4[/latex] MW Power loss: [latex]P_{Loss} = 0.001(191.4 - 50)^2 = 0.001 \times 141.4^2 \approx 20.0[/latex] MW
questions.explanation_html:
Optimal dispatch conditions:

For G1 (no transmission loss from G1):
[latex]\lambda = \dfrac{\partial C_1}{\partial P_{G1}} = 50 + 0.02P_{G1}[/latex]
[latex]70.25 = 50 + 0.02P_{G1} \Rightarrow P_{G1} = 1012.5[/latex] MW

For G2 (with loss):
[latex]\dfrac{\partial P_L}{\partial P_{G2}} = 0.002(P_{G2}-50)[/latex]
Penalty factor condition:
[latex]70.25(1 - 0.002(P_{G2}-50)) = 50 + 0.002P_{G2}[/latex]
[latex]70.25 - 0.1405P_{G2} + 7.025 = 50 + 0.002P_{G2}[/latex]
[latex]P_{G2}(0.1405 + 0.002) = 27.275 \Rightarrow P_{G2} \approx 191.4[/latex] MW

Power loss:
[latex]P_{Loss} = 0.001(191.4 - 50)^2 = 0.001 \times 141.4^2 \approx 20.0[/latex] MW

questions.question: A balanced three-phase supply is given to a 30 kW, 4-pole, 400 V, 50 Hz, wound rotor induction motor with Y-connected stator and rotor windings. The motor is driving a constant torque load. With shorted sliprings, the machine runs at 1476 rpm. When an external non-inductive resistance of 0.27 [latex]\Omega[/latex] per phase is connected in series in the rotor circuit, the steady-state speed drops to 1404 rpm. Neglecting rotational losses, the actual per phase rotor winding resistance is ____ [latex]\Omega[/latex] (Round off to two decimal places)
questions.explanation: Synchronous speed: [latex]N_s = \dfrac{120 \times 50}{4} = 1500[/latex] rpm Slip 1 (shorted): [latex]s_1 = \dfrac{1500 - 1476}{1500} = \dfrac{24}{1500} = 0.016[/latex] Slip 2 (external R): [latex]s_2 = \dfrac{1500 - 1404}{1500} = \dfrac{96}{1500} = 0.064[/latex] For constant torque , torque [latex]\propto \dfrac{r_2}{s}[/latex] = constant: [latex]\dfrac{r_2}{s_1} = \dfrac{r_2 + R_{ext}}{s_2}[/latex] [latex]r_2 \cdot s_2 = (r_2 + 0.27) \cdot s_1[/latex] [latex]r_2(s_2 - s_1) = 0.27 \times s_1[/latex] [latex]r_2(0.064 - 0.016) = 0.27 \times 0.016[/latex] [latex]r_2 \times 0.048 = 0.00432[/latex] [latex]r_2 = 0.09\ \Omega[/latex]
questions.explanation_html:
Synchronous speed: [latex]N_s = \dfrac{120 \times 50}{4} = 1500[/latex] rpm

Slip 1 (shorted): [latex]s_1 = \dfrac{1500 - 1476}{1500} = \dfrac{24}{1500} = 0.016[/latex]

Slip 2 (external R): [latex]s_2 = \dfrac{1500 - 1404}{1500} = \dfrac{96}{1500} = 0.064[/latex]

For constant torque, torque [latex]\propto \dfrac{r_2}{s}[/latex] = constant:
[latex]\dfrac{r_2}{s_1} = \dfrac{r_2 + R_{ext}}{s_2}[/latex]

[latex]r_2 \cdot s_2 = (r_2 + 0.27) \cdot s_1[/latex]
[latex]r_2(s_2 - s_1) = 0.27 \times s_1[/latex]
[latex]r_2(0.064 - 0.016) = 0.27 \times 0.016[/latex]
[latex]r_2 \times 0.048 = 0.00432[/latex]
[latex]r_2 = 0.09\ \Omega[/latex]

Concept:
For maximum power transfer, [latex] R_L=R_{th}, [/latex] where [latex]R_{th}[/latex] is the Thevenin resistance seen from the load terminals.

Step 1: Remove the load
To find the Thevenin resistance, disconnect [latex]R_L[/latex] and deactivate the independent source. Since the circuit contains only an independent voltage source, [latex] 10~\text{V} \rightarrow \text{Short Circuit}. [/latex]

Step 2: Redraw the circuit
After short-circuiting the voltage source:
  • The left terminal of the [latex]10~\Omega[/latex] resistor is connected to ground.
  • The [latex]5~\Omega[/latex] resistor is completely shorted and has no effect.
  • From the load terminals, the [latex]10~\Omega[/latex] resistor and the [latex]4~\Omega[/latex] resistor are both connected between the output node and ground.

[latex] R_{th} = \frac{10\times4}{10+4} = \frac{40}{14} = \frac{20}{7} = 2.857~\Omega. [/latex]
Rounded to two decimal places, [latex] R_{th}=2.86~\Omega. [/latex]

Step 4: Maximum power transfer
For maximum power transfer, [latex] R_L=R_{th}=2.86~\Omega. [/latex]

questions.question: Consider the circuit shown. Assume that the diode ([latex]D[/latex]) is ideal. Given [latex]v_s = 100\sin(2\pi 50t)[/latex] V, [latex]V_{dc} = 50[/latex] V, and [latex]R = 10\ \Omega[/latex], the average value of the current through the diode is ___________ A (Round off to two decimal places)
questions.explanation: Diode conducts when [latex]v_s > V_{dc}[/latex]: [latex]100\sin\theta > 50 \Rightarrow \sin\theta > 0.5 \Rightarrow \theta \in [\pi/6,\ 5\pi/6][/latex] Conducting current: [latex]i = \dfrac{v_s - V_{dc}}{R} = \dfrac{100\sin\theta - 50}{10}[/latex] Average current: [latex]I_{avg} = \dfrac{1}{2\pi}\int_{\pi/6}^{5\pi/6}\dfrac{100\sin\theta - 50}{10}\,d\theta[/latex] [latex]= \dfrac{1}{2\pi}\left[-10\cos\theta - 5\theta\right]_{\pi/6}^{5\pi/6}[/latex] [latex]= \dfrac{1}{2\pi}\left[\left(-10\times(-\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}) - \frac{25\pi}{6}\right) - \left(-10\times\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2} - \frac{5\pi}{6}\right)\right][/latex] [latex]= \dfrac{1}{2\pi}\left[10\sqrt{3} - \frac{20\pi}{6}\right] = \dfrac{5\sqrt{3}}{\pi} - \dfrac{5}{3} \approx 2.756 - 1.667 \approx 1.09[/latex] A
questions.explanation_html:
Diode conducts when [latex]v_s > V_{dc}[/latex]:
[latex]100\sin\theta > 50 \Rightarrow \sin\theta > 0.5 \Rightarrow \theta \in [\pi/6,\ 5\pi/6][/latex]

Conducting current: [latex]i = \dfrac{v_s - V_{dc}}{R} = \dfrac{100\sin\theta - 50}{10}[/latex]

Average current:
[latex]I_{avg} = \dfrac{1}{2\pi}\int_{\pi/6}^{5\pi/6}\dfrac{100\sin\theta - 50}{10}\,d\theta[/latex]

[latex]= \dfrac{1}{2\pi}\left[-10\cos\theta - 5\theta\right]_{\pi/6}^{5\pi/6}[/latex]

[latex]= \dfrac{1}{2\pi}\left[\left(-10\times(-\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}) - \frac{25\pi}{6}\right) - \left(-10\times\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2} - \frac{5\pi}{6}\right)\right][/latex]

[latex]= \dfrac{1}{2\pi}\left[10\sqrt{3} - \frac{20\pi}{6}\right] = \dfrac{5\sqrt{3}}{\pi} - \dfrac{5}{3} \approx 2.756 - 1.667 \approx 1.09[/latex] A

questions.question: The magnitude of the contour integral [latex]\oint_C \left(\dfrac{(z+1)^2}{(z-i)(z-2)}\right)dz[/latex] over the contour [latex]C: |z - 2 - i| = 3/2[/latex] is ______ (Round off to two decimal places) Note: [latex]z[/latex] is a complex variable and [latex]i = \sqrt{-1}[/latex]
questions.explanation: Contour [latex]C[/latex]: center [latex]2+i[/latex], radius [latex]1.5[/latex]. Check singularities: [latex]z = i[/latex]: distance from center [latex]= |2+i-i| = 2 > 1.5 \rightarrow[/latex] outside [latex]z = 2[/latex]: distance from center [latex]= |2-(2+i)| = 1 < 1.5 \rightarrow[/latex] inside By Residue Theorem: [latex]\oint = 2\pi i \times \text{Res}_{z=2}\dfrac{(z+1)^2}{(z-i)(z-2)}[/latex] [latex]\text{Res}_{z=2} = \dfrac{(2+1)^2}{(2-i)} = \dfrac{9}{2-i} = \dfrac{9(2+i)}{5} = \dfrac{18+9i}{5}[/latex] [latex]\oint = 2\pi i \times \dfrac{18+9i}{5} = \dfrac{2\pi(-9+18i)}{5}[/latex] [latex]\left|\oint\right| = \dfrac{2\pi}{5}\sqrt{81+324} = \dfrac{2\pi}{5}\times\sqrt{405} = \dfrac{2\pi \times 9\sqrt{5}}{5} = \dfrac{18\pi}{\sqrt{5}} \approx 25.29[/latex]
questions.explanation_html:
Contour [latex]C[/latex]: center [latex]2+i[/latex], radius [latex]1.5[/latex].

Check singularities:
[latex]z = i[/latex]: distance from center [latex]= |2+i-i| = 2 > 1.5 \rightarrow[/latex] outside
[latex]z = 2[/latex]: distance from center [latex]= |2-(2+i)| = 1 < 1.5 \rightarrow[/latex] inside

By Residue Theorem:
[latex]\oint = 2\pi i \times \text{Res}_{z=2}\dfrac{(z+1)^2}{(z-i)(z-2)}[/latex]

[latex]\text{Res}_{z=2} = \dfrac{(2+1)^2}{(2-i)} = \dfrac{9}{2-i} = \dfrac{9(2+i)}{5} = \dfrac{18+9i}{5}[/latex]

[latex]\oint = 2\pi i \times \dfrac{18+9i}{5} = \dfrac{2\pi(-9+18i)}{5}[/latex]

[latex]\left|\oint\right| = \dfrac{2\pi}{5}\sqrt{81+324} = \dfrac{2\pi}{5}\times\sqrt{405} = \dfrac{2\pi \times 9\sqrt{5}}{5} = \dfrac{18\pi}{\sqrt{5}} \approx 25.29[/latex]

questions.question: A uniform spherical volume charge distribution of radius 2 m, centered at the origin, has a strength of [latex]\dfrac{3}{\pi} \times 10^{-6}[/latex] C/m[latex]^3[/latex]. A point charge of strength [latex]\pi \times 8.854 \times 10^{-12}[/latex] C is moved from [latex](-3, 0, -4)[/latex] to [latex](0, 0, 4)[/latex] in Cartesian coordinate system. The relative permittivity of the medium is 1 and the coordinate values are in meters. The work done during the process is ______ [latex]\mu[/latex]J (Round off to two decimal places)
questions.explanation: Total sphere charge: [latex]Q_{vol} = \rho_v \times \dfrac{4}{3}\pi r^3 = \dfrac{3}{\pi} \times 10^{-6} \times \dfrac{4\pi}{3}(2)^3 = 32 \times 10^{-6}[/latex] C Point charge: [latex]q = \pi \times 8.854 \times 10^{-12}[/latex] C Distances from origin (both points outside sphere [latex]r=2[/latex]): [latex]r_1 = \sqrt{9+0+16} = 5[/latex] m (start) [latex]r_2 = \sqrt{0+0+16} = 4[/latex] m (end) Work done: [latex]W = q(V_2 - V_1) = q \times \dfrac{Q_{vol}}{4\pi\epsilon_0}\left(\dfrac{1}{r_2} - \dfrac{1}{r_1}\right)[/latex] [latex]= \pi \times 8.854 \times 10^{-12} \times \dfrac{32 \times 10^{-6}}{4\pi \times 8.854 \times 10^{-12}}\left(\dfrac{1}{4} - \dfrac{1}{5}\right)[/latex] [latex]= \dfrac{32 \times 10^{-6}}{4} \times \dfrac{1}{20} = 8 \times 10^{-6} \times 0.05 = 4 \times 10^{-7}[/latex] J [latex]= 0.40\ \mu[/latex]J
questions.explanation_html:
Total sphere charge:
[latex]Q_{vol} = \rho_v \times \dfrac{4}{3}\pi r^3 = \dfrac{3}{\pi} \times 10^{-6} \times \dfrac{4\pi}{3}(2)^3 = 32 \times 10^{-6}[/latex] C

Point charge: [latex]q = \pi \times 8.854 \times 10^{-12}[/latex] C

Distances from origin (both points outside sphere [latex]r=2[/latex]):
[latex]r_1 = \sqrt{9+0+16} = 5[/latex] m (start)
[latex]r_2 = \sqrt{0+0+16} = 4[/latex] m (end)

Work done:
[latex]W = q(V_2 - V_1) = q \times \dfrac{Q_{vol}}{4\pi\epsilon_0}\left(\dfrac{1}{r_2} - \dfrac{1}{r_1}\right)[/latex]

[latex]= \pi \times 8.854 \times 10^{-12} \times \dfrac{32 \times 10^{-6}}{4\pi \times 8.854 \times 10^{-12}}\left(\dfrac{1}{4} - \dfrac{1}{5}\right)[/latex]

[latex]= \dfrac{32 \times 10^{-6}}{4} \times \dfrac{1}{20} = 8 \times 10^{-6} \times 0.05 = 4 \times 10^{-7}[/latex] J [latex]= 0.40\ \mu[/latex]J

questions.question: Let [latex]X[/latex] and [latex]Y[/latex] be two real-valued random variables with [latex]E(X)=1[/latex], [latex]E(Y)=2[/latex], [latex]E(X^2)=4[/latex], [latex]E(Y^2)=9[/latex], and [latex]E(XY)=0.9[/latex], where [latex]E[/latex] denotes the expectation operator. The value of [latex]\alpha[/latex] that minimizes [latex]E\left((X - \alpha Y)^2\right)[/latex] is __________ (Round off to one decimal place)
questions.explanation: Expand the objective: [latex]f(\alpha) = E\left((X - \alpha Y)^2\right) = E(X^2) - 2\alpha E(XY) + \alpha^2 E(Y^2)[/latex] [latex]= 4 - 2\alpha(0.9) + 9\alpha^2[/latex] [latex]= 9\alpha^2 - 1.8\alpha + 4[/latex] Minimise by differentiating and setting to zero: [latex]\dfrac{df}{d\alpha} = 18\alpha - 1.8 = 0[/latex] [latex]\alpha = \dfrac{1.8}{18} = 0.1[/latex] Answer: 0.1
questions.explanation_html:
Expand the objective:
[latex]f(\alpha) = E\left((X - \alpha Y)^2\right) = E(X^2) - 2\alpha E(XY) + \alpha^2 E(Y^2)[/latex]
[latex]= 4 - 2\alpha(0.9) + 9\alpha^2[/latex]
[latex]= 9\alpha^2 - 1.8\alpha + 4[/latex]

Minimise by differentiating and setting to zero:
[latex]\dfrac{df}{d\alpha} = 18\alpha - 1.8 = 0[/latex]
[latex]\alpha = \dfrac{1.8}{18} = 0.1[/latex]

Answer: 0.1

questions.question: The integral [latex]\dfrac{1}{\pi}\int_0^{\infty} \dfrac{x^{2026}}{(1 + x^{2026})(1 + x^{2})}\,dx[/latex] evaluates to _________ (Round off to two decimal places)
questions.explanation: Let [latex]I = \dfrac{1}{\pi}\int_0^{\infty}\dfrac{x^n}{(1+x^n)(1+x^2)}dx[/latex] where [latex]n = 2026[/latex]. Also define: [latex]J = \dfrac{1}{\pi}\int_0^{\infty}\dfrac{1}{(1+x^n)(1+x^2)}dx[/latex] Step 1: [latex]I + J = \dfrac{1}{\pi}\int_0^{\infty}\dfrac{1}{1+x^2}dx = \dfrac{1}{\pi} \times \dfrac{\pi}{2} = \dfrac{1}{2}[/latex] Step 2: Substitute [latex]x \to 1/x[/latex] in [latex]I[/latex]: [latex]I = \dfrac{1}{\pi}\int_0^{\infty}\dfrac{x^{-n}}{(1+x^{-n})(1+x^{-2})}\dfrac{dx}{x^2} = \dfrac{1}{\pi}\int_0^{\infty}\dfrac{1}{(x^n+1)(1+x^2)}dx = J[/latex] Step 3: Since [latex]I = J[/latex]: [latex]2I = \dfrac{1}{2} \Rightarrow I = \dfrac{1}{4} = 0.25[/latex] Answer: 0.25
questions.explanation_html:
Let [latex]I = \dfrac{1}{\pi}\int_0^{\infty}\dfrac{x^n}{(1+x^n)(1+x^2)}dx[/latex] where [latex]n = 2026[/latex].

Also define: [latex]J = \dfrac{1}{\pi}\int_0^{\infty}\dfrac{1}{(1+x^n)(1+x^2)}dx[/latex]

Step 1: [latex]I + J = \dfrac{1}{\pi}\int_0^{\infty}\dfrac{1}{1+x^2}dx = \dfrac{1}{\pi} \times \dfrac{\pi}{2} = \dfrac{1}{2}[/latex]

Step 2: Substitute [latex]x \to 1/x[/latex] in [latex]I[/latex]:
[latex]I = \dfrac{1}{\pi}\int_0^{\infty}\dfrac{x^{-n}}{(1+x^{-n})(1+x^{-2})}\dfrac{dx}{x^2} = \dfrac{1}{\pi}\int_0^{\infty}\dfrac{1}{(x^n+1)(1+x^2)}dx = J[/latex]

Step 3: Since [latex]I = J[/latex]:
[latex]2I = \dfrac{1}{2} \Rightarrow I = \dfrac{1}{4} = 0.25[/latex]

Answer: 0.25

questions.question: Consider a linear arrangement of seven bulbs, each of which can be in the ON or OFF states. The initial configuration of the bulbs is shown in the figure. In every Step, the states of the bulbs are changed based on the following rules: Any OFF bulb with exactly one ON neighbor at the end of the previous Step is turned ON. Any ON bulb with both neighbors ON at the end of the previous Step is turned OFF. The state of any bulb not meeting the conditions above is left unchanged. Initial: ON ON ON OFF ON ON ON Step 1: ON ON OFF OFF OFF ON ON Step 2: ON OFF OFF ON OFF OFF ON The number of bulbs which are ON at the end of Step 8 is ______
questions.explanation: Step-by-step Transition: Step 1: For bulb 3 (OFF), it has one ON neighbor (bulb 2). It turns ON. For bulb 5 (ON), both neighbors (bulbs 4 and 6) are ON. It turns OFF. New configuration after Step 1: [1,1,1,0,0,1,1] Step 2: For bulb 4 (OFF), it has exactly one ON neighbor (bulb 5 was OFF). It turns ON. For bulb 6 (ON), both neighbors (bulbs 5 and 7) are OFF. So, it remains ON. New configuration after Step 2: [1,1,1,1,0,1,1] Continuing similarly, we perform this process up to Step 8, applying the rules repeatedly: [1,1,1,1,0,1,1] -> [1,1,1,0,1,1,1] -> [1,1,0,1,1,0,1] ... and so on. Finally, after Step 8, the bulb configuration is determined to be: [0,1,1,0,1,0,1] Counting the number of ON bulbs at Step 8 gives us 4.
questions.explanation_html:
Step-by-step Transition:
Step 1:
For bulb 3 (OFF), it has one ON neighbor (bulb 2). It turns ON.
For bulb 5 (ON), both neighbors (bulbs 4 and 6) are ON. It turns OFF.
New configuration after Step 1: [1,1,1,0,0,1,1]

Step 2:
For bulb 4 (OFF), it has exactly one ON neighbor (bulb 5 was OFF). It turns ON.
For bulb 6 (ON), both neighbors (bulbs 5 and 7) are OFF. So, it remains ON.
New configuration after Step 2: [1,1,1,1,0,1,1]
Continuing similarly, we perform this process up to Step 8, applying the rules repeatedly: [1,1,1,1,0,1,1] -> [1,1,1,0,1,1,1] -> [1,1,0,1,1,0,1] ... and so on.
Finally, after Step 8, the bulb configuration is determined to be: [0,1,1,0,1,0,1]
Counting the number of ON bulbs at Step 8 gives us 4.

questions.question: [latex]P[/latex] and [latex]Q[/latex] are two positive integers such that [latex]P^{2} = Q^{2} + 13[/latex]. The product of the numbers [latex]P[/latex] and [latex]Q[/latex] is _________
questions.explanation: [latex]P^{2} - Q^{2} = 13[/latex] [latex]\Rightarrow (P-Q)(P+Q) = 13[/latex] Since 13 is prime and [latex]P, Q[/latex] are positive integers: [latex]P - Q = 1[/latex] and [latex]P + Q = 13[/latex] Solving: [latex]P = 7,\ Q = 6[/latex] Product [latex]= 7 \times 6 = 42[/latex]
questions.explanation_html:
[latex]P^{2} - Q^{2} = 13[/latex]
[latex]\Rightarrow (P-Q)(P+Q) = 13[/latex]

Since 13 is prime and [latex]P, Q[/latex] are positive integers:
[latex]P - Q = 1[/latex] and [latex]P + Q = 13[/latex]

Solving: [latex]P = 7,\ Q = 6[/latex]

Product [latex]= 7 \times 6 = 42[/latex]
